paragraphs: The natural order of the subject leads us to consider next the provision of the Constitution that authorizes the national legislature to regulate, in the last resort, the election of its own members. It reads: "The TIMES, PLACES, and MANNER of holding elections for senators and representatives shall be prescribed in each State by the legislature thereof; but the Congress may, at any time, by law, make or alter SUCH REGULATIONS, except as to the PLACES of choosing senators."(1) This provision has been denounced not only by those who condemn the Constitution wholesale, but also by those who have objected with less sweeping force and greater moderation. In one instance it has been thought objectionable even by a gentleman who has declared himself the advocate of every other part of the system.

I am greatly mistaken, nevertheless, if there is any article in the whole plan more completely defensible than this one. Its propriety rests on the evidence of this plain proposition: EVERY GOVERNMENT OUGHT TO CONTAIN IN ITSELF THE MEANS OF ITS OWN PRESERVATION. Every just reasoner will approve at first sight an adherence to this rule in the work of the Convention. He will disapprove every departure from it that does not appear to have been dictated by the necessity of incorporating into the work some particular ingredient with which strict conformity to the rule was incompatible. Even in that case, though he may accept the necessity, he will not cease to regard, and to regret, a departure from so fundamental a principle as a portion of imperfection in the system, which may prove the seed of future weakness and perhaps of anarchy.

It will not be claimed that an election law could have been framed and inserted in the Constitution that would always have fit every probable change in the situation of the country. It will therefore not be denied that a discretionary power over elections ought to exist somewhere. It will, I presume, be as readily conceded that there were only three ways in which this power could reasonably have been arranged and placed. It must have been lodged either wholly in the national legislature, or wholly in the State legislatures, or primarily in the latter and ultimately in the former. The last mode has, with reason, been preferred by the Convention. They have submitted the regulation of elections for the federal government in the first instance to the local administrations, which in ordinary cases, and when no improper views prevail, may be both more convenient and more satisfactory. But they have reserved to the national authority a right to step in whenever extraordinary circumstances might make that intervention necessary for its safety.

Nothing can be more evident than that an exclusive power to regulate elections for the national government, in the hands of the State legislatures, would leave the existence of the Union entirely at their mercy. They could annihilate it at any moment by neglecting to provide for the choice of the persons who administer its affairs. It is to little purpose to say that such a neglect or omission would not be likely to occur. The constitutional possibility of the thing, without an equivalent for the risk, is an unanswerable objection. Nor has any satisfactory reason yet been given for running that risk. The extravagant surmises of a distempered jealousy can never be dignified with that name. If we are in a humor to presume abuses of power, it is as fair to presume them on the part of the State governments as on the part of the general government. And since it is more consonant with the rules of sound theory to trust the Union with the care of its own existence than to transfer that care to any other hands, then if abuses of power are to be risked on one side or the other, it is more rational to risk them where the power would naturally be placed than where it would unnaturally be placed.

Suppose an article had been put into the Constitution empowering the United States to regulate the elections for the individual States. Would any man have hesitated to condemn it, both as an unwarranted transfer of power and as a deliberate engine for the destruction of the State governments? The violation of principle in that case would have needed no comment, and to an unbiased observer it will be no less apparent in the project of making the existence of the national government, in a similar respect, depend on the pleasure of the State governments. An impartial view of the matter cannot fail to produce a conviction that each, as far as possible, ought to depend on itself for its own preservation.

As an objection to this position, it may be remarked that the make-up of the national Senate would involve, in its full extent, the danger that is said to flow from an exclusive power in the State legislatures to regulate the federal elections. It may be alleged that by declining to appoint senators they might at any time strike a fatal blow at the Union. From this it may be inferred that since the Union's existence would thus be made to depend on them in so essential a point, there can be no objection to entrusting them with it in the particular case under consideration. The interest of each State in keeping its representation in the national councils, it may be added, would be a complete security against an abuse of the trust.

This argument, though plausible, will not on examination prove sound. It is certainly true that the State legislatures, by refusing to appoint senators, may destroy the national government. But it does not follow that because they have a power to do this in one instance, they ought to have it in every other. There are cases in which the harmful tendency of such a power may be far more decisive, without any motive as cogent as the one that must have governed the Convention in forming the Senate to recommend admitting it into the system. So far as that arrangement exposes the Union to the possibility of injury from the State legislatures, it is an evil. But it is an evil that could not have been avoided without shutting the States, in their political capacities, wholly out of a place in the organization of the national government. Had that been done, it would doubtless have been interpreted as an entire abandonment of the federal principle, and it would certainly have deprived the State governments of the absolute safeguard they will enjoy under this provision. But however wise it may have been to accept a problem in this instance to gain a necessary advantage or a greater good, no inference can be drawn from it in favor of piling up the evil where no necessity urges and no greater good invites.

It may easily be seen also that the national government would run a much greater risk from a power in the State legislatures over the elections of its House of Representatives than from their power to appoint the members of its Senate. The senators are to be chosen for six years. There is to be a rotation by which the seats of a third of them are vacated and refilled every two years. No State is to be entitled to more than two senators, and a quorum of the body is to consist of sixteen members. The joint result of these circumstances would be that a temporary combination of a few States to suspend the appointment of senators could neither destroy the existence of the body nor impair its activity. And it is not from a general and permanent combination of the States that we can have anything to fear. The first might proceed from sinister designs in the leading members of a few of the State legislatures. The last would presuppose a fixed and rooted disaffection in the great body of the people, which will either never exist at all or will in all probability come from experience of the inability of the general government to advance their happiness, in which event no good citizen could desire its continuance.

But with regard to the federal House of Representatives, a general election of members is intended once every two years. If the State legislatures were given an exclusive power to regulate these elections, every time they were held would be a delicate crisis in the national situation. It might end in a dissolution of the Union if the leaders of a few of the most important States had entered into a prior conspiracy to prevent an election.

I shall not deny that there is some weight in the observation that the interest of each State in being represented in the federal councils will be a security against abuse of a power over its elections in the hands of the State legislatures. But those who attend to an obvious distinction will not consider the security complete: the distinction between the interest of the people in the public happiness and the interest of their local rulers in the power and consequence of their offices. The people of America may be warmly attached to the government of the Union at times when the particular rulers of particular States, stimulated by the natural rivalry of power and by hopes of personal aggrandizement, and supported by a strong faction in each of those States, may be in a very opposite temper. This difference of feeling between a majority of the people and the individuals with the greatest credit in their councils is exemplified in some of the States at the present moment, on the present question. The scheme of separate confederacies, which will always multiply the chances of ambition, will be a never-failing bait to all such influential characters in the State administrations as are capable of preferring their own personal gain and advancement to the public welfare. With so effective a weapon in their hands as the exclusive power to regulate elections for the national government, a combination of a few such men in a few of the most considerable States, where the temptation will always be strongest, might accomplish the destruction of the Union. They need only seize the opportunity of some casual dissatisfaction among the people (which perhaps they may themselves have stirred up) to discontinue the choice of members for the federal House of Representatives. It ought never to be forgotten that a firm union of this country, under an effective government, will probably be an increasing object of jealousy to more than one nation of Europe, and that enterprises to subvert it will sometimes originate in the intrigues of foreign powers and will seldom fail to be encouraged and abetted by some of them. Its preservation, therefore, ought in no case that can be avoided to be committed to the guardianship of anyone but those whose situation will uniformly give them an immediate interest in the faithful and vigilant performance of the trust.
